From hotels allegedly used as hideouts by internet fraudsters to secret sex parties, drug dealings and violent encounters, hotel workers share disturbing experiences within the hospitality industry, VICTOR AYENI writes Aside from being a nail technician, Patience Benita (not her real name) works part-time as a sex worker in Lekki, Lagos – a trade which, though illegal in some parts of Nigeria, makes her a familiar face in the nightlife scene. Like every other day, she receives messages from several male admirers on Facebook , a social networking platform with over three billion active users. But last month, the 25-year-old received a message from an account bearing the name Ola (surname withheld), with a few photos of a young man who appeared to be in his mid-20s. Benita, who happened to be quite streetwise, chalked this up to the typical online persona of most “Yahoo boys.” This was the beginning of an exchange that lasted three days before moving to WhatsApp , a more private platform where the man suggested he preferred to chat with her. Perhaps picking up clues that she was a sex worker, one morning, Ola asked how much she would charge to spend some time with him. “I told him N200,000, and he was silent for a while before responding, ‘Okay.’ I was surprised. He was supposed to negotiate and try to bring the price down, but he didn’t,” Benita told Saturday PUNCH. Benita said she had mixed feelings about this. A part of her felt somewhat suspicious that something was not adding up, while another part of her saw Ola as a ‘lucky customer’ who might even pay her more than she had asked for. About 30 minutes into the chat, Ola gave her the name of a popular hotel along the Lekki-Ajah axis and asked Benita to meet him there. “I was doing some laundry that day because it was a Saturday, but he kept blowing up my phone with calls. I explained to him that I would be on my way as soon as I was done washing. After that, I took a commercial motorcycle to the hotel. “He then took me to the room he had booked and asked me to make myself comfortable, saying he wanted to freshen up. He then entered the bathroom. Because of my earlier suspicions, I had prepared myself before going to the hotel. “Out of curiosity, I looked under the bed and saw that there was something he had placed underneath it. I didn’t express any fear; I played it cool. So, when he came back to the room, we started making out and took off our clothes,” Benita recounted. ‘He tried to use me for rituals’ After the sexual act was complete, she said her client began to hurry her up, urging her to put her clothes back on quickly because he was expecting a visitor. As she stepped out of the room and descended the few steps leading out of the hotel, the 26-year-old described feeling a sudden disorientation. “I started to feel a very sharp pain in my stomach, and at the same time, my vision was becoming blurry. Ola accompanied me to the hotel gate and bade me goodbye. I managed to walk for a while before I got to a roundabout where there was a police checkpoint. Then I started throwing up. “The police officers came to my aid and kept asking me what had happened, but I couldn’t talk. As this was happening, passers-by began to gather around me and sympathise with me. One of them was a man who spoke to me in a language, and I realised he knew where I was from. ‘I responded in our native language and asked him to help me open my bag and bring out my phone because I no longer had the physical strength to do so. When he did, he helped me dial the number of a native doctor,” Benita said. Saturday PUNCH learnt that when the native doctor got wind of what had happened, he told her that Ola had tried to use her for money rituals. Owing to the urgency of the situation, he instructed Benita over the phone on the materials to obtain and the necessary chants to recite. The belief in a form of ‘money rituals,’ in which a person drains the physical life from another individual through voodoo, which is believed to translate into sudden material wealth, is rife across cultures in Nigeria. Benita believes that this was what Ola intended to do with her, in addition to the sexual encounter they had. “Part of what he told me to do involved water, and I followed the instructions. The doctor told me the guy wanted to use me for rituals and that what I would drink would serve as an antidote and neutralise it. I drank the water. “The man helped me call a cab and accompanied me to the car. He told the driver where I was going. That was how I left the place, and the pain and dizziness subsided. I went home, had my bath and slept,” Benita recalled. When asked if she would stop sex work and how the incident had changed her, Benita sighed. “I have got rid of this client’s contact. I wonder if what he tried to use me for later bounced back on him. But since that day, I have been more careful with my hustle. “I now advise my girls to prepare themselves because we don’t know the real intentions of these Yahoo boys looking for hookups. I don’t know if these guys have specific hotels they use or choose random ones, so one just has to be careful and spiritually fortified,” she noted. An unsolved murder In June last year, the body of a woman, identified as Aladi Johnson, was found in a hotel in Abuja, although the circumstances leading to her death have remained unknown. The victim was found with her hands bound behind her back and was unclad from her waist down, while the tight black dress she wore was slightly exposed at her back. According to a statement signed by the FCT Police Public Relations Officer, Josephine Adeh, a preliminary investigation revealed that the victim, a female from Benue State, checked into the hotel located at Third Avenue, Gwarinpa, on June 16, in the company of an unidentified male who was later observed to have exited the premises without her. She added that the victim was discovered unconscious by hotel staff during routine service rounds, prompting immediate notification to the police. However, a hotel receptionist, who preferred to be called Charles Iwunde, told Saturday PUNCH that such a tragedy must have been masterminded by a criminal who has observed flaws within the hotel’s internal security protocols. The 30-year-old explained that criminals who carry out such crimes in hotels must have observed that there was no compulsory identity verification for guests or that the functional surveillance systems would not capture their identities. “How come the hotel workers saw the suspect leaving without the lady he came in with, and nobody called immediately to check? This can only happen if the place is a motel for ‘short time’ fun, or the guy has been lodging there and bringing different ladies before he finally struck. There are situations like this, and they are usually done by Yahoo boys. “They lodge in hotels and spend weeks. They smoke and bring in all kinds of ladies, sometimes more than three. I don’t know if they perform anything fetish in there, but it’s common knowledge that they host parties in halls and from there lodge in rooms. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Though some of them are rude and aggressive with us because they believe they can do whatever they want,” Iwunde noted. On Monday, 26 young men were reportedly arrested at a hotel in Aradagun, Olorunda Local Council Development Area, following a joint operation by soldiers and police operatives. The suspects were nabbed over allegations of fraudulent online business and overseas employment activities. Reports indicate that more than 100 youths, mostly between the ages of 20 and 28, had been lodging at the hotel in connection with the fraudulent online business. Keeping sealed lips To several hotel staffers who spoke with Saturday PUNCH , the proclivity of hotel guests to engage in debauchery and use illegal drugs is one of the many dark secrets lurking behind working in the hospitality industry. A graduate in Akure, Ondo State, Timileyin Asuni (not his real name) said he worked part-time in a hotel without his parents’ knowledge. “One day, my father walked in with a small girl. He knew it was me, but I didn’t indicate it. I greeted him pleasantly and attended to him. When he was leaving, he called my native name. I didn’t respond; I just maintained my composure, but I was raging within. “That’s what the work entails. Even if someone brings in your babe, you must not complain; you smile and attend to them, then when you get home, you can start tackling the issue,” Asuni said. “Working in a hotel is like moving through a hole of secrets; your eyes will just be seeing many things,” a former room service attendant who preferred to be called Anthony Olajere disclosed. In 2024, Olajere started working at a four-star hotel in Ikeja as a receptionist. He was responsible for welcoming guests, collecting guests’ details, assigning rooms and issuing room keys or access cards. According to him, the position exposed him to a wide range of what happens within hotel rooms, but staffers are prohibited from speaking about such incidents unless they involve serious criminal offences. “You will see some men coming with young girls, and some married women too coming with guys, and you must serve them; you can’t say a thing. The profession doesn’t allow it. It was hotel work that made me sceptical about marriage. “There was this client, a married woman, who would lodge almost every morning with a young guy, who should be in his 20s. This woman is married and, from the way she’s attired, it appears she pretends to go to work every morning, but she comes to the hotel with this guy. “As a service attendant, you are not professionally allowed to gossip about any guest, even if it’s someone you know. You can’t exchange phone contacts with them or engage them in personal conversations. But you find some ladies who will slip their numbers to you, or make passes at you even while beside their men,” he recounted. Illegal drugs Olajere noted that he was privy to some other sexually explicit encounters involving some guests and staff, which he said are facilitated by money. When asked why he left the hotel within a year, after some hesitation, he admitted that he was caught on camera frequently sneaking into a guest’s room. “He is a Yahoo boy; he comes from outside the country and stays regularly in that hotel. He had my number. One day, I got a call from him, and he requested cannabis, which I helped him obtain. It continued like that for a while, and we started to talk, and he gave me some money. “One day, my supervisor invited me into the Managing Director’s office, and I was shown different CCTV footage of me entering his room. They asked what I was always doing in his room, and I had to confess since there was evidence showing me going in there. “They said I was enabling criminal behaviour and terminated my appointment. But this is not new; many guests bring illegal drugs into hotel rooms, but the thing is, they must not get caught. And if you catch them in it, they will most likely bribe you to keep mute,” Olajere revealed. Cannabis is illegal in Nigeria under federal laws such as the Indian Hemp Act and the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency Act. Cultivating or trafficking it can attract severe penalties. Underground sex parties A hotel bartender who simply gave his name as Henry revealed that some hotels and guest houses are rented for wild sex parties, particularly during weekends. He clarified that in recent times, following police intervention after violent outbreaks at some of these parties, many of the organisers have preferred to rent short-let apartments, lounges and bars, especially on Lagos Island. “These parties are often very coded, and the locations are not known until a few hours before they start. These are adult parties, and everything happens there. Talk about sex, drugs and cocktails, they happen. Their organisers usually distribute condoms and lubricants to the guests. “These do not happen in all hotels. There’s usually a sort of agreement between the hotel managers and the organisers of these parties, and lots of money is involved. Though many of these parties now prefer short-lets, where there is less possibility of police intrusion. “During COVID-19, some of these hotel parties were being raided by state officials for not following social distancing protocols, so the organisers have gone more underground now. Some of these parties have passwords, codes or particular attire required to gain entry, and the locations are well guarded,” Henry said. A flier for one such party to be held on a weekend this month was forwarded to our correspondent. The location was said to be discreet until the night of the event, but a source familiar with the organisers disclosed that it was most likely going to be on Lagos island. Participants were asked to come wearing masks and were promised the opportunity to enjoy games, music and drinks. Interested participants were provided with an account number and asked to pay a sum of N60,000 each. Our correspondent also saw a flier for a ‘Strippers Night’ that was held in a hotel in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, earlier this month. The details of the hotel address, along with the phone numbers and social media handles of the hotel, were indicated on the flier. In September 2022, the Anambra State Government, through the Ministry of Culture, Entertainment and Tourism, closed down a hotel in Ifite, Awka, over a viral sex party that was allegedly held in the hotel. Explicit videos of the party reportedly emerged online, where people could be seen having sex while some were watching and recording the sex acts on their phones. Following the sealing of the hotel, the state government said it had commenced an investigation into the event. Fights over lovers Like other shades of human behaviour, physical altercations between women or men also occur in hotels – most frequently stemming from romantic rivalries, interpersonal disputes, and hotel bill disagreements. Recounting his experience, a receptionist in a hotel on Lagos Island, Dayo Akinfe (not his real name), said he was on duty one evening last year when he helped a man and a lady who arrived, and he lodged both of them in an upstairs room. But for some odd reason, the two love birds requested a change of room to another one downstairs. But in this room, Akinfe had earlier lodged a couple. “As we were changing the room, the man in the downstairs room and his lady saw the other lady from the upstairs room with her man, and a fight broke out; he started to yell. Turned out that this lady was his fiancée. “How both couples came to the same hotel on the same night and by coincidence met was surprising. The funny thing was that after the bitter quarrel, each lover went inside and had their fun. I wonder what would befall that relationship after then,” Akinfe said. Also speaking with Saturday PUNCH, a hotel worker in Ibadan, Oyo State, Yetunde Ajao (not her real name) disclosed that he once saw the husband of her friend bring a lady to the hotel where she worked. “This man didn’t know I saw them, but I did. Once I confirmed their room number, I tipped my friend. This man had been maltreating my friend, and she had once lamented to me how her husband had neglected her. “I told her the room number – which I know is against the rules of our profession – and she went there to cause havoc. It was a big fight. The other lady had her clothes turned into shreds. It was not a good scene,” Ajao said. Secrets of a church hotel When Chris Udoh (not his real name) got a job as a housekeeper at a guest house owned by his church in a community in Rivers State, he was excited. At the time, the 22-year-old had been awaiting admission into a university in Port Harcourt and found the prospect of making some money while working at the church’s retreat centre an admirable offer. But that excitement soon began to fade as the reality of the job began to dawn on him. Three particular experiences, however, stood out among the many he had. In one, a man and a woman from a certain church had lodged at the hotel and requested some olive oil. “I was naïve; I thought they wanted to pray with it. I rushed to the street close to our hotel and bought some for them. Initially, I had wanted to lodge them in a room on the second floor, but they insisted on the third floor, so I gave them a comfortable room there. “I didn’t know when they left, but they most likely sneaked out. When I entered the room, I saw the oil sprinkled everywhere, the bed had been moved, the bedsheets were intertwined, and the duvet was wrinkled. It was as if they had had violent sex,” Udoh recounted. He also recounted the case of a man and a woman who lodged at the church hotel but, due to the strict policies in place, had to be assigned separate rooms because they were not married. “We put the man in Room 002 and the woman in Room 005, but the next day, after they checked out, the rooms and bathrooms were soiled with used and unused condoms and semen,” Udoh recalled, shaking his head. In yet another experience that was far from conventional, he recounted an incident involving a guest from Asaba, Delta State, who arrived in the company of two young men, supposedly to attend a church programme in the town. “The man appeared to be in his early 40s, while the other two guys seemed to be in their late 20s – apparently his work boys. After setting up the room, they lodged there. But when I entered the room to give them towels and bars of soap, one of them was looking at me in a very strange way. “I noticed that he was holding his crotch and licking his lips as he made eye contact with me, but I ignored that. Again, when I was about to step out of the bathroom, this particular guy was standing at the door with his hand placed across the wall, so I said ‘excuse me’ and left the place,” Udoh recounted. After receiving a phone call from the man who lodged the young men, instructing him to keep an eye on his boys, Udoh recalled receiving one more phone call from one of the guests requesting a third pillow for them. But this was not the end of it. The third phone call was from this same man to his personal line, and the conversation made Udoh very uncomfortable. “He was calling me ‘fine boy’, asking me questions like where I live, how I have fun, do I like swimming and then the odd one: can we hang around sometime? He was even asking me to book another hotel for him close by, saying he would give me money to do that, and then invite him. “At this point, I realised this man wanted to do disgusting stuff with me, and that was why he brought those two guys. I was irritated by how he kept harassing me after that day, but I starved him of any attention. The next day, when I went to clean the room where the guys stayed in, I saw both used and unused condoms and the pillow smelled badly. I don’t know what they did with it,” Udoh said. As he cleaned the room, he recalled initially second-guessing himself, wondering whether it was later occupied by a man and a woman. But it was clear that the three guests he had lodged in that room were men. “When I reported this to my supervisor, I had to be discreet about what I disclosed, telling him instead that the men brought in girls. He was livid that some people were using a church-owned guest house for unholy acts. But I know what happened in there was more than unholy,” Udoh said. ‘I saw men having sex’ As a hotel receptionist, William Opara loved his job and was dedicated to the wellness of their guests. But one day, a sight he encountered while at his job shocked him out of his socks. Recounting his experience to Saturday PUNCH, he recalled that the incident occurred in 2022, specifically, in the month of August at a hotel in Lagos. Two guests who were known to regularly lodge in their hotel every weekend came one Friday evening like they usually do. Opara had always assumed that they were business partners who stayed together, perhaps for a meeting close to the area where the hotel was situated. “I always prepare their room for them, ensure that it is well cleaned and everything in it is working fine. That day, one of them complained to me that the tap in the bathroom was not flushing properly. “I called the manager to brief him on what was happening, and he instructed me to go check what was going on. There were some other urgent calls I received that delayed me from going immediately. “Now, when I got to the room where these two men stayed, I knocked, but there was no answer. The door wasn’t locked from the inside, so I opened it and walked in, and there they were, both having sex, which I think is best left undescribed. “I was so shocked that I was wondering if my eyes were deceiving me or actually seeing what I saw. I never believed stuff like this happened in here in our country until that day,” Opara recounted. Opara said he quickly entered the bathroom to check on the tap in a bid to ward off the shock, and when he stepped out of there after a while, one of the men called on him. “He pleaded with me not to tell people what I had seen about them. He was covered up now. Reaching for his phone, he asked for my details, sent me a huge amount of money and told me not to alert anyone. “Till I resigned from that hotel, these two men were still coming there for their stuff. They should be in their late 20s. I learned that they were Yahoo boys,” he added. Stakeholders condemn harbouring criminals In April, the National President of Nigeria Hotel Association, Patrick Anyanwu, warned members nationwide against accommodating criminals in their hotels. He added that any hotelier found harbouring criminals, including internet fraud suspects, could face sanctions which could include possible closure. “Any hotelier caught harbouring criminals or ‘Yahoo Yahoo’ boys will have themselves to blame. The association believes in the standard operating system that adheres to the dictates of the industry,” Anyanwu said. Speaking with Saturday PUNCH, a hotel supervisor, Biyi Ologun, stated that the hospitality sector accommodates people regardless of their identities, but criminals should not be given a place to hide within hotels. He further stated that hotel staff should not encourage actions that may have fatal consequences for the health and safety of other guests. “Guests should also respect the rules that guide the hospitality industry and understand that these rules were made to protect us. Guests should also be careful meeting strangers from social media, because they could be criminals seeking someone to harm. “You should always inform a trusted friend or family member of your exact location, the hotel’s name, the room number, and the identity of the person you are meeting. “And when hotel employees observe suspicious behaviour, they should not overlook it or cover up crime. They must report immediately to the hotel security, the Nigeria Police Force, or the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons,” Ologun noted.
